items.elicits: Student must commit to a symbol for 3/4 vs 5/8 and then write the basis for it: rename 3/4 as 6/8 and compare eighths, or argue from a picture or from both fractions' position relative to 1/2. The denominators are related (8 is a multiple of 4), so the renaming is a single step.

Student must compare 2/3 and 7/12 where the benchmark 1/2 does not separate them (both exceed it), so a workable strategy has to be renaming to twelfths (8/12 vs 7/12) or a model; the written work shows which strategy was actually run.

Student must compare 5/6 and 8/9 where neither denominator is a multiple of the other: either build eighteenths (15/18 vs 16/18) or reason about the missing piece from one whole (1/6 vs 1/9). The strategy choice has consequences here, and the shown work exposes it.

diagnosis.supports: Under proctoring, individually, with only paper and pencil and on number pairs the students had not seen, the teacher may conclude that the student selected a valid comparison strategy, carried it out, and wrote reasoning that connects to the symbol recorded.
does_not_support: It does not reach strategy flexibility or efficiency: a student may run one method (common denominators) on all three pairs, so the evidence does not show that benchmarks or visual models are available to that student.

It does not reach the adjacent claim it is most likely to be mistaken for — ordering three or more fractions, or placing fractions on a number line — since every item is a two-fraction pairwise comparison.

The symbol on its own is a one-in-three choice among <, > and =, so where a student's shown work is missing, thin or illegible, that item's mark alone does not separate a chosen strategy from a lucky guess; only the written reasoning does that work.
It does not reach a general justification of why the strategy works (why renaming preserves the amount), only its correct application to these three pairs.

delegation.reason: The comparisons are worked in the room under proctoring with paper and pencil on numbers the students had not seen, and each item requires the student's own written route to the symbol, not just the symbol.

components.component: Chooses a valid comparison strategy (equivalent fractions, a benchmark such as one half, or a visual model)
components.evidence: Part A instruction: 'Then show how you know (a common denominator, a picture, or a benchmark like 1/2)' leaves the choice to the student rather than prescribing a method.

components.component: Executes the chosen strategy on the pair
components.evidence: Items 1-3 require an actual comparison to be carried out; item 3 (5/6 vs 8/9) cannot be settled by the 1/2 benchmark and forces a renaming or a distance-from-one argument.

components.component: Shows the reasoning that supports the symbol written
components.evidence: 'For each pair, write <, >, or =. Then show how you know'; the header also states 'Show all work'.

gate1_components.why: Every component of this claim is exercised by items 1-3: the strategy is left to the student, the pairs (including one whose denominators are not multiples) force it to be executed, and the reasoning is required in writing alongside the symbol. Nothing named in the claim is absent, so Gate 1 fails and there is no gap here.

gate2_materiality.why: Not reached: Gate 1 failed because no component of the claim is unexercised.

gate3_value.why: Not reached: analysis stopped at Gate 1.

diagnosis.why_no_gap: The assessment sets out to carry this claim and does: three unseen pairs, a free strategy choice, execution, and written reasoning tied to the symbol, all produced under supervision. The remaining limits (single method per student, pairwise only) are the ordinary boundaries of the claim as written, not holes in it.

items.elicits: Renaming 3/4 into eighths to set two fractions in like-sized parts before comparing them.
Building twelfths from thirds so that 2/3 and 7/12 are expressed in like-sized parts and can be compared directly.
Finding a common denominator for sixths and ninths, where neither denominator is a multiple of the other, and comparing the renamed parts.
Renaming halves and thirds into sixths and combining like parts: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6, with the steps written out.
Renaming sixths and fourths into twelfths and subtracting like parts: 10/12 - 3/12 = 7/12; the operation runs in the harder direction (subtraction) with unlike parts.
Handling mixed numbers: renaming 1/3 and 3/4 as twelfths, adding to 13/12, and regrouping the improper part into the whole to give 4 1/12.
Deciding from a described situation that the two distances combine, renaming to twelfths, adding to 19/12, and regrouping to the mixed number 1 7/12 as the item explicitly demands.
Reading a 'how much more' situation as a subtraction, renaming thirds and fourths to twelfths, and taking the difference: 8/12 - 3/12 = 5/12.

diagnosis.supports: Under proctoring, individually, on paper, with unseen numbers, the teacher may conclude that the student can build a common denominator for unlike fractions, combine or compare the like-sized parts in both addition and subtraction, including with mixed numbers, and regroup an improper result into a mixed number where the item calls for it.
does_not_support: It does not reach reduction to lowest terms: none of the answers produced by items 4-8 (5/6, 7/12, 4 1/12, 1 7/12, 5/12) is reducible, so a correct paper here is not evidence that the student can simplify a result such as 6/8 or 10/12, even though 'Answers in simplest form' is printed on the page.

It does not reach the adjacent claim it is most likely to be mistaken for — fluency or automaticity with unlike denominators — since eight items in twenty-five minutes with all work written speaks to accuracy on a small set, not to speed or to holding up across a wider range of denominators.
It does not reach multiplication or division of fractions, or addition of three or more unlike fractions; every item combines exactly two quantities.
In Part A the symbol itself is a one-in-three selection, so for those items the common-denominator work only counts as evidence where the student actually wrote it.

delegation.reason: Every step is written in the room under proctoring with paper and pencil on number pairs the students had not seen, so a submitted paper is the student's own execution rather than a retrievable result.

components.component: Constructs equivalent fractions with a common denominator
components.evidence: Items 4-8 all pair unlike denominators (2 and 3; 6 and 4; 3 and 4; 4 and 6; 3 and 4), and Part A permits a common denominator as the route.

components.component: Combines or compares like-sized parts
components.evidence: Part B 'Add and subtract' and Part C word problems require the combination; Part A requires the comparison of renamed parts.

components.component: Regroups an improper result into a mixed number where the item requires it
components.evidence: Item 6 (2 1/3 + 1 3/4) yields 13/12 over the whole numbers, and item 7 says 'write your answer as a mixed number' for a sum of 19/12.

components.component: Simplifies a result to lowest terms where the item requires it
components.evidence: The instruction 'Answers in simplest form' appears in Part B, but no item produces a reducible answer: 4 gives 5/6, 5 gives 7/12, 6 gives 4 1/12, 7 gives 1 7/12, 8 gives 5/12. The claim itself conditions this on 'where the item requires it', and no item does.

gate1_components.why: Three of the four components are exercised repeatedly. The fourth, simplification, is not absent from the assessment so much as not called for by it: the claim's own wording is conditional ('where the item requires it') and no item's answer is reducible, so its non-appearance is a scope fact about these numbers rather than a hole. Nothing qualifies to carry forward, so Gate 1 fails.

gate2_materiality.why: Not reached: Gate 1 failed, since no component that materially belongs and narrows support was found absent.

gate3_value.why: Not reached: analysis stopped at Gate 1.

diagnosis.why_no_gap: This assessment sets out to carry the procedural claim and does so across five worked items plus the Part A renaming, in both operations and with mixed numbers, under conditions that make the work observed. The one unexercised element, simplification, is conditional in the teacher's own wording and no item triggers it.
diagnosis.over_verified_note: Common-denominator construction is exercised eight times across Parts A, B and C. That is more instances of one move than the claim needs; if anything on this page is redundant burden inside twenty-five minutes, it is the repetition of that single step, not any thin spot.

items.elicits: Given a worked wrong answer (1/2 + 1/4 = 2/6), the student must locate the error in someone else's reasoning and write what it was, then produce the correct sum 3/4. The prompt asks what the student did wrong; naming the move ('they added the bottoms', 'they needed a common denominator') answers it, and an account of why sixths are the wrong-sized part is invited by 'explain' but not required by it.

diagnosis.narrower_inference: Under supervision the student can identify, in an unseen worked example, that the denominators were added instead of a common denominator being found, and can produce the correct sum.
diagnosis.supports: The teacher may conclude that the student recognises the added-denominators error when it is shown to them and can correct the computation, on a case they had not seen before, without help.
does_not_support: It does not reach the mechanism the claim names — why the resulting sixth is the wrong-sized part — because a response that names the error and computes 3/4 satisfies the item without ever referring to the size of the pieces.

It does not reach the adjacent claim it is most likely to be mistaken for: spotting the error when it is presented is not the same as not committing it, nor as catching it unprompted in one's own work, and items 4-8 do not offer the temptation because no distractor is present there.

It does not reach transfer of the misconception's logic to subtraction (a student writing 1/2 - 1/4 = 0/2 is never elicited) or to any other denominator pair; one instance with halves and fourths is the whole basis.
It does not reach whether the student can say what 2/6 would be the correct answer to, i.e. what quantity the wrong procedure actually computes.

delegation.reason: The explanation is written by hand in the room under proctoring on a worked error the students had not seen, so whatever appears is the student's own account.

diagnosis.gap_statement: We cannot tell from item 9 whether a student who names the error can say why adding denominators yields a part of the wrong size, since naming the rule that was broken earns the item just as fully as explaining the size of the parts.

components.component: Identifies the error in the worked example (the denominators were added rather than a common denominator found)
components.evidence: 'A student added 1/2 + 1/4 and got 2/6. Explain what the student did wrong' puts the erroneous work in front of the student and asks for the error.

components.component: States why adding denominators produces a wrong-sized part
components.evidence: No item asks about the size of the parts. Item 9 asks 'what the student did wrong', which is answered by naming the move; nothing on the page requires the student to say that sixths are smaller pieces than the fourths and halves being combined, or that the answer 2/6 is smaller than 1/2 alone.

components.component: Gives the correct sum
components.evidence: 'and show the correct answer', with the header instruction 'Show all work'.

gate1_components.carried_forward: States why adding denominators produces a wrong-sized part
gate1_components.why: Two of the three components are exercised by item 9. The third is the explanatory half of the claim and is the one the teacher wrote most specifically ('states why ... a wrong-sized part'); the item's question is a different question, about what was done rather than about why the resulting part is the wrong size, and it is not carried anywhere else on the page. It materially belongs to this claim, the teacher has not said it is assessed elsewhere, and its absence narrows what the paper licenses, so it is carried forward as the single component.

gate2_materiality.why: This is the diagnostic claim, and its whole point is the mechanism of the misconception. A correct item 9 saying 'they added the bottoms, the answer is 3/4' will read on the page exactly like the evidence the teacher wants, so she would credit an account of part size that the paper never asked for and may not contain. That is a conclusion the evidence does not carry.

gate3_value.why: It is specific to this item's wording rather than the ordinary narrowness of any one-item claim: the gap is between the question asked ('what did the student do wrong') and the claim as confirmed ('states why ... produces a wrong-sized part'), which a teacher reading finished papers has little occasion to notice, because the responses she credits will look right. It is also the only claim of the three where what the paper produces falls short of the wording, so it is not a general caution about single items.

diagnosis.missing_evidence: The assessment produces no written account of why the parts are the wrong size — no item requires the student to say that sixths are smaller pieces than the halves and fourths being combined, or that 2/6 is less than 1/2 on its own, so the papers contain identification of the error and the corrected sum but nothing that shows the reasoning behind either.

items.item: Prompt question: 'What is the author's point of view on replacing the Mill Street bridge, and how does the author respond to the opposing case?'
items.elicits: The student must commit to one reading of the whole passage and assert a stance, rather than summarise what the passage is about.

items.item: Task bullet 1: 'State the author's point of view in your own words (do not just say "the author is against it").'
items.elicits: The student must render the stance in her own language, which blocks a bare pro/con tag and forces her to say what the author is actually for and against.

items.item: Task bullet 3: 'For each piece of evidence, explain how it shows the author's position.'
items.elicits: The student must trace the stance back to a specific authorial choice instead of asserting it, i.e. show the route from text to position.

diagnosis.narrower_inference: The student can state the author's position on replacing the bridge accurately and in her own words, and can connect that position to specific choices in the text.
diagnosis.supports: Under proctored, individual conditions with an unseen passage, a teacher may conclude that the student read this passage closely enough to state the author's position in her own words and to tie it to particular moves in the text.
does_not_support: It does not reach a stance that is genuinely unstated: the passage closes with 'I am not sure the numbers are the only thing that should be counted,' so an accurate position statement here may be a paraphrase of the author's own sentence rather than an inference from the text's choices.
It is easily mistaken for the adjacent claim 'identifies the author's purpose or main idea' — one accurate stance statement about one editorial passage is not that broader claim.

It says nothing about transfer: one passage, on one occasion, in a paragraph structure and rubric the teacher reports are already familiar, so it does not reach the student's stance-reading on a second text or a different informational genre.
It does not reach evaluation of the stance — whether the author's position is well founded, or whether the student can weigh it against the engineer's — which the paragraph never asks for.

delegation.reason: The paragraph is hand-written in the room in one 45-minute period with only the passage and paper, on a passage the teacher states is new to the students, so the thinking that produced the words happened where the teacher could see it.

diagnosis.gap_statement: We cannot tell from a paragraph that states the position and cites supporting evidence whether the student inferred the author's position from the text's choices or read it off the closing sentence 'I am not sure the numbers are the only thing that should be counted.'

components.component: States the author's position on replacing the bridge in the student's own words

components.component: Ties that position to specific choices the author made in the text

gate1_components.carried_forward: Arrives at the position from the author's choices rather than from a sentence in which the author states it
gate1_components.why: The first two components are exercised by explicit task bullets and are present. The third is the one the teacher's own wording insists on ('rather than from any sentence that states it'), it is not carried anywhere else, and its absence changes what the paragraph licenses, so it is the single component carried forward.

gate2_materiality.why: The claim as confirmed turns on the position being unstated. Because this passage half-states it in the first person and nothing in the task separates the two routes, a teacher reading an accurate stance statement would conclude the student inferred the position from the text's choices, when the paragraph does not carry that distinction.

gate3_value.why: This is not the ordinary narrowness of a single-passage task; it is a property of this particular passage that a teacher who wrote the claim as 'unstated' may not have registered, and it changes how she reads the first sentence of every paragraph she scores.

diagnosis.missing_evidence: This assessment does not produce any observation that separates a position reached from the author's choices from a position paraphrased out of the passage's closing first-person sentence.

items.item: Task bullet 2: 'Quote or closely paraphrase two pieces of textual evidence that reveal the author's point of view.'
items.elicits: The student must select spans on the criterion of revealing stance rather than of being about the topic, and must reproduce them accurately — a selection judgment, not a retrieval.

items.item: Task bullet 3: 'For each piece of evidence, explain how it shows the author's position (word choice, contrast, placement, or what the author chooses to include).'
items.elicits: The student must name the mechanism carrying the stance for each selected piece and state how that mechanism does the work.

items.item: Rubric rows 2 and 3: 'Two relevant pieces of evidence' and 'Explanation connects each piece of evidence to the point of view'
items.elicits: Two evidence-plus-mechanism pairings rather than one worked example plus a second citation left bare.

diagnosis.supports: Under proctored, individual conditions on an unseen passage, a teacher may conclude that the student can pick two stance-revealing pieces of text and say, for each, by what technique it signals the author's position.
does_not_support: It does not reach command of the full technique range the claim lists: the student chooses her two pieces, and both may run on the same mechanism, so nothing here shows she can recognise, say, omission when contrast is not available.

It is easily mistaken for the adjacent claim that the student can evaluate evidence — whether the two pieces are the strongest ones in the passage, or whether they actually justify the author's position, is never asked.

The 4-point rubric does not isolate technique-naming (its third row scores only that the explanation connects evidence to the point of view), so a total score cannot stand in for this claim; the paragraph's own wording is the evidence for it.

It does not reach unprompted selection: the task states in advance that two pieces are wanted and supplies the technique vocabulary in parentheses, so it is not evidence that the student would look for stance signals in a text without being told to.

delegation.reason: Both the selection and the explanation are written by hand in class from a passage the students had not seen, with no resource beyond the passage itself, so the selecting is done in the room.

components.evidence: 'For each piece of evidence...' and rubric: 'Explanation connects each piece of evidence to the point of view (1)'.

The narrowness that remains — one passage, the student's own choice of technique — is the ordinary reach of a single 45-minute task and is recorded in does_not_support rather than as a hole.

items.item: Prompt question, second half: '...and how does the author respond to the opposing case?'
items.elicits: The student must treat the engineer's case as a position in its own right and locate the author's move against it, not merely report that a disagreement exists.

items.item: Task bullet 4: 'Explain how the author acknowledges and responds to the engineer's case for replacement.'
items.elicits: The student must reconstruct the engineer's case from the second paragraph (tired steel, narrow deck, two-thirds the cost, twenty years against seventy-five) and then say what the author does with it — grants it, then reframes what the inspection report measures.

items.item: Rubric row 4: 'Accurately describes how the author handles the opposing view (1)'
items.elicits: Both halves — the acknowledgement and the answer — rather than one of the two.

diagnosis.supports: Under proctored, individual conditions on an unseen passage, a teacher may conclude that the student can find where an author grants an opposing case and can describe the move by which the author answers it.
does_not_support: It does not reach evaluation: whether the author's answer to the engineer is fair, adequate, or leaves the cost argument standing is never asked.

It is easily mistaken for the adjacent claim that the student understands counterargument and rebuttal as a structure — this passage hands the opposing case its own paragraph and flags the turn with 'What the engineer did not mention', which is a more legible arrangement than most argument texts offer.
It does not reach production: nothing here shows the student can acknowledge and answer an opposing case in her own argument writing.
One passage on one occasion does not reach consistency; it says nothing about a text where the opposing case is scattered or only implied.

delegation.reason: The description must be written in class from a passage the students had not seen, so identifying the engineer's case and the author's answer to it happens under supervision.

components.component: Identifies the engineer's case as the passage presents it

gate1_components.why: Both halves the teacher named — acknowledges, and answers — are asked for explicitly in bullet 4 and scored in the rubric's fourth row, and the material each half needs is present in the passage. No component is absent, so Gate 1 fails and there is no gap.

gate2_materiality.why: Not reached: Gate 1 failed, so no absence was carried forward to test for materiality.

gate3_value.why: Not reached: Gate 1 failed, so nothing reached this gate.

diagnosis.why_no_gap: This claim is carried in substance. Bullet 4 asks for exactly the two moves the claim names, the rubric scores them, and the observation is produced in the room on a new passage. That it is one instance of a clearly signposted counterargument is a limit on reach, noted in does_not_support, not an absence in the assessment.

items.elicits: The student must add three trial values and divide by three for each of four rows, then write each result rounded to the nearest hundredth into the correct cell.
The student must construct a plot from the four averaged pairs, place height on the x-axis and speed on the y-axis, choose a workable scale, and write a unit on each axis label.

diagnosis.supports: Under proctored, individual, no-AI conditions the teacher may conclude that this student, unaided, computed the four averages to the stated precision and produced a speed-against-height graph with both axes labelled with units.
does_not_support: It does not reach whether the student can collect or design the measurement: the trial data was gathered collectively by the class and handed to every student pre-made.
It does not reach interpretation of the graph's shape; drawing a correct curve is a plotting act, and reading a diminishing-increment pattern off it is claimed separately (S2c/S4c).
It does not reach arithmetic fluency without tools, since a calculator is a permitted resource and the averaging may be entirely machine-performed.
No item here is selected-response, so no answer on this claim can be obtained by guessing among supplied options; the guess-rate caveat does not apply to S1c.

delegation.reason: The averaging and the graph are drawn on paper in a proctored, individual sitting with AI prohibited and enforced, so the marks on the page were made by the student in the room.

items.elicits: The student must move from describing the pattern to accounting for it, writing a causal chain in which height at release sets the gravitational potential energy and that energy becomes kinetic energy at the bottom, using the two named energy terms.

diagnosis.supports: Under these conditions the teacher may conclude that this student, unaided, produced a grade-appropriate written explanation of the observed pattern in terms of gravitational potential energy becoming kinetic energy.
does_not_support: It does not reach whether the student would identify energy transfer as the relevant framework unprompted, because item 5 names gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy and instructs the student to use them.

It does not distinguish a genuine transfer account from a fluent restatement of the two supplied terms attached to the pattern already described in items 3 and 4.
It does not reach transfer of the explanation to a different energy context, such as a pendulum or a falling object; the observation is confined to this ramp.

delegation.reason: The explanation is composed on paper during a supervised 30-minute individual sitting with AI prohibited and enforced, so no outside author can have written it.

gate2_materiality.why: The assessment's own instruction announces simplest form, and a correctly completed paper will be entirely in simplest form, so the teacher would reasonably read a clean paper as confirmation that students simplify. She would have to check the reducibility of every answer key entry to discover otherwise, so this materially limits the summative inference she intends to draw.

gate3_value.why: This is a fact about the particular numbers in her item set rather than the ordinary narrowness every assessment carries; it is not something an experienced teacher would assume, since the presence of the simplest-form instruction points the other way, and it bears directly on an end-of-unit summative judgment.

items.elicits: Adding 2 1/3 and 1 3/4 leaves thirteen twelfths in the fractional position, so the student must notice the fractional part has reached or passed one whole and move that whole across into the whole-number part.

diagnosis.supports: Under proctoring with these numbers new to the students, the teacher may conclude that a student recognises an improper result and rewrites it as a whole number with a proper fractional remainder, both when the item names that form and when the item leaves the student to notice it.
does_not_support: It does not reach the reverse conversion, rewriting a mixed number as an improper fraction, which item 6 permits as a route but never requires.

It does not reach regrouping in the subtraction direction, that is borrowing a whole to make a subtraction possible, since no item on the paper requires it; this is the adjacent claim this evidence is most likely to be mistaken for.
It does not reach whether the student can say what the mixed number means as a quantity, only that the rewriting is performed.

It does not reach improper results well past one whole or with denominators outside this range; both instances here resolve to a single whole plus a remainder. No item bearing on this claim is selected-response, so no guess-rate caveat applies.
